chapterNote: Haman is dead, but his sealed decree still stands — and by Persian law it cannot be repealed. So deliverance comes not by cancelling the death-warrant but by issuing a second, equal one: the Jews may gather and defend their lives. The very rigidity of Medo-Persian law that once doomed them now shields them. Mordecai rides out in royal blue and gold, and the mourning of chapter 4 turns to light and gladness across the empire.

1.text: That same day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told how he was related to her.

2.text: The king took off his signet ring, which he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai; and Esther set Mordecai over the estate of Haman.
2.notes: The ring of absolute authority passes from the enemy of the Jews to a Jew. Everything Haman built to destroy Mordecai — rank, house, the king's seal — is now handed to Mordecai himself. The reversal is total.

3.text: Then Esther spoke to the king once more. She fell at his feet, weeping, and begged him to avert the evil of Haman the Agagite and the scheme he had devised against the Jews.

4.text: The king held out the golden scepter to Esther, and she rose and stood before him.

5.text: "If it please the king," she said, "and if I have found favor before him, and the thing seems right to the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let an order be written to revoke the letters that Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite devised and wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king's provinces.

6.text: For how can I bear to watch the disaster that will fall on my people? How can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?"
6.notes: Esther's plea is not for herself — her own life is now secure — but wholly for her people. Having risked death to be counted among them, she cannot rest while they remain under sentence. This is the intercessor's heart: safety is no comfort while the flock is in danger.

7.text: King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "See, I have given Esther the estate of Haman, and they have hanged him on the gallows because he laid his hand on the Jews.

8.text: Now write concerning the Jews in the king's name whatever seems good to you, and seal it with the king's signet ring — for an edict written in the king's name and sealed with his ring cannot be revoked."
8.amp: a writing which is written in the king's name and sealed with the king's ring, no one may revoke [le-hashiv — to turn back, reverse].
8.notes: Here the book's great legal knot is cut. The first decree cannot be unmade — 'no one may revoke' it — so the answer is a second decree of equal, irreversible force. The same unbending law of the Medes and Persians that nearly destroyed the Jews (1:19; 3:12) is turned into the very instrument of their rescue.

9.text: So the king's secretaries were summoned at that time, in the third month (that is, the month of Sivan), on the twenty-third day; and it was written, just as Mordecai commanded, to the Jews, and to the satraps, governors, and officials of the provinces from India to Cush — a hundred and twenty-seven provinces — to each province in its own script and each people in its own language, and to the Jews in their own script and language.

10.text: Mordecai wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus, sealed it with the king's signet ring, and sent the letters by mounted couriers riding the swift royal steeds bred from the king's own stables.

11.text: By these letters the king granted the Jews in every city the right to assemble and defend their lives — to destroy, kill, and annihilate any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, with their children and women, and to plunder their goods —
11.notes: The wording deliberately mirrors Haman's decree (3:13), but its force is defensive: the right to stand and be defended rather than be slaughtered unresisting. What the enemy meant for extermination is answered, clause for clause, with permission to live.

12.text: on a single day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus — the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar.

13.text: A copy of the writing was to be published as law in every province and made known to all the peoples, so that the Jews would be ready on that day to avenge themselves on their enemies.

14.text: The couriers, mounted on the royal steeds, went out in urgent haste at the king's command, and the decree was issued in the fortress of Susa.

15.text: Mordecai went out from the king's presence in royal robes of blue and white, wearing a great crown of gold and a mantle of fine linen and purple; and the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.
15.notes: Mordecai, who sat in sackcloth at the gate (4:1–2), now goes out crowned in royal blue and gold. The clothing marks the reversal: the mourner is exalted, and the city that reeled in confusion at Haman's decree (3:15) now rings with joy.

16.text: Light and gladness had come to the Jews, with joy and honor.
16.amp: the Jews had light [orah] and gladness [simchah], joy [sason] and honor [yeqar].

17.text: And in every province and every city, wherever the king's command and decree reached, there was gladness and joy among the Jews, with feasting and celebration. And many of the peoples of the land became Jews, for the fear of the Jews had fallen on them.
17.notes: The deliverance draws outsiders in: seeing whose side is winning — and, beneath the surface, whose God is unmistakably at work — many Gentiles cast their lot with the covenant people. The hidden Hand has grown visible enough to convert.
